title: A* on a grid
sub: Dijkstra with aim: heuristics for 4 and 8 directions, admissibility and consistency, tie-breaking, struct nodes and a search number, NavMesh and Jobs
cards/0/title: The problem, and the game dev interview question behind it
cards/0/body:
Shortest Path in Binary Matrix (LeetCode #1091). An n × n grid, n ≤ 100: 0 is free, 1 is a wall. Find the shortest path from the top-left corner to the bottom-right one over free cells, moving in 8 directions, with a diagonal costing the same as a straight step. The length is the number of cells on the path, start and finish included. No path — return −1.

All steps cost the same, so BFS from the unit on graphs solves it. But in a Unity interview it stands for "explain A*" — the most common algorithm question in game dev. The signals that you need A* rather than Dijkstra or BFS:

1. There is one goal, known in advance.
2. There is geometry: coordinates let you estimate how much is left.
3. The map is large and searches are frequent — one per unit per click.
cards/1/q: An open field with no walls, 8 directions, a diagonal costs 1. The unit is in the middle, the goal is 100 steps away diagonally. How many cells do Dijkstra or BFS expand before they reach the goal?
cards/1/options/0: ≈ 4·10⁴ — every cell closer than 100 steps, in all directions
cards/1/options/1: ≈ 100 — only the cells on the diagonal to the goal
cards/1/options/2: ≈ 10⁴ — the quarter of the square that faces the goal
cards/1/explain: Dijkstra expands cells in increasing g and does not know where the goal is. For a goal 100 away it expands every cell with g < 100 — a square of side 199, about 4·10⁴, while the path is 100 cells. That is 400 times more work than needed, and it is what A* fixes.
cards/1/wrong/1: 100 cells is the path itself. But Dijkstra has no sense of direction: the wave spreads equally in all directions.
cards/1/wrong/2: Dijkstra prefers no side — the expansion order depends only on g, and the square around the unit is symmetric.
cards/2/body:
Dijkstra picks the cell with the smallest g, the distance travelled from the start. A* adds h, an estimate of what is left to the goal, and takes the smallest f = g + h from the heap: an estimate of the whole path through that cell. Cells "behind" get a large h and wait; the wave stretches towards the goal. With h = 0 it is Dijkstra.

Which h to use depends on how the unit moves (dr, dc are the row and column differences to the goal):

4 directions — Manhattan: dr + dc.
8 directions, a diagonal costs 1 (as in #1091) — Chebyshev: max(dr, dc).
8 directions, a diagonal costs √2 — octile: max + (√2 − 1)·min; with integer costs 10 and 14 — 10·max + 4·min.
Any angle — Euclidean distance.

On an empty map each of them is exactly the remaining path for its movement model. With walls the real path is longer and h underestimates it — which is how it should be.
cards/3/body:
An admissible h never overestimates: h ≤ the true remainder. Then, when the goal leaves the heap, its g is the shortest: every unfinished path in the heap has f ≤ its true length, so a shorter path would have come out earlier.

A consistent (monotone) h never jumps by more than a step's cost: h(a) ≤ cost(a, b) + h(b). Then f never decreases along a path, and a cell that leaves the heap is already final — as in Dijkstra. The code relies on it: closed cells are never touched again. A consistent h is always admissible; the four heuristics from the previous card are consistent for their movement models.

Overestimating breaks the guarantee. Manhattan with 8 directions: from (0, 0) to (1, 1) it says 2, while it is one step. A cell may close with too large a g, and the path comes out longer than the shortest. In exchange, fewer cells are expanded.

Sometimes that is a deliberate trade: weighted A* with f = g + w·h, w > 1, pulls towards the goal more greedily and finds a path no longer than w × the shortest. For a horde of enemies, "nearly shortest" at twice the speed is often the right call; for a route hint shown to the player, it is not.
cards/4/q: A straight step costs 10, a diagonal 14, with 8 moves. Which h is admissible and exactly equal to the remaining cost on an empty map?
cards/4/explain: The optimal path on an empty map is min(dr, dc) diagonals at 14 plus the rest straight: 14·min + 10·(max − min) = 10·max + 4·min. That is octile: exact, and it never overestimates.
cards/4/wrong/1: Manhattan counts a diagonal as two straight steps, 20 instead of 14: an overestimate, so the path may come out longer than the shortest.
cards/4/wrong/2: Chebyshev is admissible, but it prices a diagonal at 10 instead of 14 — an underestimate, so A* expands more cells than it has to.
cards/5/title: How A* is written in a game: structs, a search number and a key
cards/5/body:
Nodes are structs in an array indexed by cell, r·n + c, not a class Node with a Parent field. An object per cell is an allocation, garbage for Boehm, and pointer chasing that misses the cache. An array of structs is allocated once and laid out contiguously.

The closed set is a search number. A node's Opened and Closed fields store the number of the search that marked them. A new search does search++, and every old mark is out of date at once. There is no need to clear an array of 10⁶ cells before every search.

The heap key is one long: f in the high bits, then h, then the cell number (20 bits — up to 2²⁰ ≈ 10⁶ cells). On equal f, the smaller h comes out first — the cell nearer the goal. That is tie-breaking: on an open field hundreds of cells share the same f, and without it A* would expand them all; with it, it heads straight for the goal.

In #1091 the length counts cells while g counts steps: the answer is g + 1.
cards/6/q: Assemble the main loop of A*.
cards/6/explain: A cell already closed in this search can only come out again from a stale entry — skip it. The goal left the heap, so its g is final, and the length in cells is g + 1. A neighbour already open in this search with a g that is no worse is left alone. The key takes f = g + h: with h alone it is greedy best-first search, not A*.
cards/7/task: Step through A* with the Chebyshev heuristic on a 7 × 7 map. In a cell: g at the top left, h at the top right, f in the middle; the heap is the "open set" list. The rig asks twice which cell is expanded next. At the end compare: A* expanded 18 cells, Dijkstra needs 36.
cards/7/goal/asks/0/q: The heap has three entries with f = 7: (1, 2) with g = 2 and h = 5, and (0, 1) and (1, 0) with g = 1 and h = 6. Which cell is expanded next?
cards/7/goal/asks/0/explain: The key compares f, and on equal f, h. (1, 2) has the smaller h = 5: it is nearer the goal. That is tie-breaking: among cells with the same path estimate, A* takes the one that has got further, instead of fanning out over the whole tie.
cards/7/goal/asks/1/q: We expanded (2, 3), which opened (2, 4) and (3, 2) with g = 4, h = 4, f = 8 — the goal is close. The heap still holds (0, 1) with g = 1, h = 6. What is expanded next?
cards/7/goal/asks/1/explain: f decides, not h: (0, 1) has f = 1 + 6 = 7 < 8. A* has to check whether a path through (0, 1) could be 7 long — that is why it finds the shortest path and greedy search by h alone does not. (1, 0), with the same f = 7 and h = 6, loses only on the cell number, the third part of the key.
cards/8/task: The same map, but h = Manhattan — with 8 directions it overestimates a diagonal. Watch the number of expanded cells and the g values on the path; at the end the rig asks what the path will be.
cards/8/goal/asks/0/options/0/label: A path of 10 cells — the shortest, as with Chebyshev
cards/8/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: A path of 11 cells — longer than the shortest
cards/8/goal/asks/0/q: The goal (6, 6) is open with g = 10, and only 12 cells have been expanded. What will the answer be when the goal leaves the heap?
cards/8/goal/asks/0/explain: Manhattan counts a diagonal as 2. Cell (2, 0) got f = 2 + 10 = 12 and was never expanded, so (4, 2) closed with g = 5, while through (2, 0) and (3, 1) it is 4 steps away. The one-step error rode all the way to the goal: 11 cells instead of 10. Faster — 13 expansions against 18 — but wrong: overestimating strips A* of its guarantee.
cards/9/q: The object keeps nodes and search between calls. The first search on the map from the rig returns 10, and the second one on the same map returns −1. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/9/explain: Closed stores a search number, not a flag. In the second search search = 2, but cells closed in the first one still have Closed = 1 — not zero, so the code treats them as closed. The start is expanded, every neighbour is "already closed", the heap runs dry, and the answer is −1. Compare with the current number: nb.Closed == search.
cards/10/title: NavMesh versus a grid, and thousands of agents
cards/10/body:
NavMesh. The graph's vertices are not cells but convex polygons of the walkable surface — orders of magnitude fewer. Unity finds a path on the NavMesh with A* over the polygons, and the agent then follows the resulting corridor, steering towards the next visible corner. NavMeshAgent computes its path asynchronously — until it is ready, pathPending is true; NavMesh.CalculatePath computes it on the spot.

A grid is better when the world is cells anyway (tiles, strategy, roguelike), cells have different costs, the map changes every turn, or you need determinism for a networked game. NavMesh is for 3D levels with slopes, stairs and free movement.

Many agents. 1. Spread across frames: at most N searches per frame, the rest wait in a queue. 2. Jobs + Burst: a search is an IJob, node fields and the heap are NativeArrays, every job has its own scratch arrays, and the jobs run on all cores. 3. Many units with one goal — that is no longer A* but one field for everybody: the next lesson.
cards/10/deep:
An admissible but inconsistent h. Then f may decrease along a path, and a closed cell is sometimes found again more cheaply. To keep the path shortest it is reopened — pushed back into the heap; code that never touches closed cells may return a longer path with such an h. That is why games use consistent heuristics, and the four standard ones are.

Jump Point Search. On a grid with uniform cell costs a path has many symmetric variants — the same diagonals and straights in a different order. JPS drops symmetric neighbours and "jumps" along straight lines to the points where a real choice appears; on open maps it expands several times fewer cells and gives the same answer. It does not work with varying cell costs.

Hierarchy. HPA* splits the map into clusters and precomputes paths between their entrances: a long path is searched on a small graph of entrances, and the details only inside the clusters it passes. For large open worlds this is standard, and the same thought drives flow fields by chunks in the next lesson.

Key packing limits. In the key (f << 40) | (h << 20) | cell the cell and h get 20 bits each, and f gets 23 bits below the sign bit. A map up to 1024 × 1024 with a step cost of 1 fits; with 10/14 costs and larger maps the fields are widened or the heap stores a struct.

Unity profiling. If A* jobs take longer than a frame in the profiler, do not wait for them in the same Update: Schedule in one frame, Complete in the next. Allocator.Persistent buffers live for the whole level and are freed in OnDestroy.
cards/11/q: Unity, a 1024 × 1024 map. The profiler shows every A* call first spends about a millisecond clearing the closed array with Array.Clear, and the search itself is short. What do you do?
cards/11/options/0: Store a search number in each node and do search++ instead of clearing
cards/11/options/1: Keep closed cells in a HashSet<int> and call Clear
cards/11/options/2: Allocate a new bool array for every search
cards/11/explain: A search number makes "clearing" O(1): a new value of search, and every old mark is unequal to it at once. Cells are touched only when the search actually reaches them.
cards/11/wrong/1: HashSet<int> pays for a hash and a chain check on every access, and its Clear also walks the bucket arrays — across the whole capacity it once grew to.
cards/11/wrong/2: A new array of 10⁶ cells is a megabyte of garbage per search: frequent Boehm collections mean hitches, and the new memory still has to be zeroed.
cards/12/q: You are asked to explain A* in a Unity interview. Put the steps of your answer in order.
cards/12/items/0: Clarify: grid or NavMesh, 4 or 8 directions, the diagonal cost, one goal or many
cards/12/items/1: Baseline: Dijkstra or BFS expand cells by g in all directions — that is expensive
cards/12/items/2: Idea: a heap ordered by f = g + h, where h estimates the rest of the way
cards/12/items/3: Choose h for the movement model, and the condition: admissible and consistent
cards/12/items/4: Implementation: structs in an array, a search number instead of clearing, ties broken by h
cards/12/items/5: Cost: in the worst case like Dijkstra, O(E log V); on an open map little more than the path
cards/12/items/6: Scale: spread over frames, Jobs + Burst, a shared goal means a flow field
cards/12/explain: First agree on the movement model — h depends on it. Then the baseline and its cost, the idea, the condition on h — and only then the engineering part a Unity interviewer expects from a senior: memory, allocations, and what to do with a thousand agents.
